title: Ten-thousand-year-old posts and boards rest twenty metres down in a German lake
dek: Divers recovered worked timbers from Lake Arendsee that may be the oldest wooden structures yet found in Central Europe.
body: A diver's lamp picks out a vertical post rising from the mud, its top still showing the angled cuts of a stone axe. Around it lie split boards up to 1.3 metres long, their surfaces smoothed by tools that have not existed for ten millennia. The wood rests twenty metres below the surface of Lake Arendsee in Saxony-Anhalt, preserved by a geological accident that sank the ancient shoreline instead of burying it in silt.

The State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology of Saxony-Anhalt announced the finds after spring 2026 investigations. State archaeologist Harald Meller said the worked pieces are spectacular precisely because Mesolithic wood almost never survives. Until now, evidence of buildings from this period in Central Germany existed only as soil discolourations where posts once stood.

Project manager Marcel Weiß said the timbers could belong to huts or to a completely unknown type of structure. If they turn out to be permanent dwellings, they would predate the first farming longhouses in Central Europe by roughly three thousand years. That would force a rethink of how mobile hunter-gatherer communities actually lived.

The lake's unusual geology made the preservation possible. An underlying salt dome causes the lakebed to subside slowly, lowering the ancient shore beneath the water without the heavy sediment cover that usually destroys or hides such sites. A remotely operated vehicle from the Fraunhofer IOSB-AST in Ilmenau mapped the drowned landscape with high-resolution sonar, recording the precise position of each timber.

Lake Arendsee has already yielded Neolithic fish weirs, a medieval cargo vessel and a dugout canoe. The new finds push the archaeological record back to the early Mesolithic, around 10,500 years ago, when people hunted, gathered and fished the shoreline. The region is also known for the Bad Dürrenberg shaman burial, a rare glimpse of ritual life from the same period.

Researchers have not yet determined whether the posts and boards formed walls, platforms, fish traps or something else entirely. The recovery of felling marks on a 1.6-metre post and the deliberate splitting of boards show woodworking skill, but the overall plan of the structure remains invisible beneath the sediment.

Ongoing work aims to map concentrations of material that could reveal the layout of a settlement. Each new timber plotted by the ROV narrows the search for the next dive. The question is whether the site holds a single structure or the scattered remains of generations of lakeside activity.
doesnt_show: The finds do not yet show the full plan or function of the structure, nor whether it was a permanent dwelling or a seasonal feature.
settle: A complete plan of the timber layout recovered through further underwater excavation would settle the structure's form and purpose.
